newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania's Berisha accuses rivals of criminal links.
newsitem.headline: Albania's Berisha accuses rivals of criminal links.

text.p: Albanian President Sali Berisha, defending his violence-torn five-year record before next week's general election, accused his Democratic Party's Socialist rivals on Sunday of links with the criminal world.

A heart surgeon who once served the hard-line Commnunist leadership under Enver Hoxha, Berisha was touring towns in his native northern region as part of a high-profile campaign to keep intact the huge majority his party won last year.

"I call on the Socialist Party to renounce its alliances with paid criminals and follow the path of reconciliation," Berisha, his voice reduced to a rasping growl after a day's campaigning, told a rally in the town of Vau I Dejes.
"Be patient. Do not lose confidence in democracy. It is a long road, but a secure one. It is the way towards Europe."

Berisha's job is not at stake in next Sunday's legislative elections. But the contest will expose how Europe's poorest country views his pro-market drive, stained by the lawlessness unleashed after angry investors blamed him for their lost life savings sunk into failed investment schemes.
Like most events organised by Berisha and Socialist leader Fatos Nano, Sunday's rally near a giant hydroelectric station 110 km (70 miles) north of Tirana was carefully stage managed.
Several dozen supporters screamed slogans in front of an improvised stage while hundreds watched proceedings in stifling mid-afternoon heat with little enthusiasm.

Earlier on Sunday, state television said Berisha's visit to Bajram Curri, a town near his village birthplace, was disrupted by gunmen firing into the air before his arrival. It said he later spoke to "continuous ovations" from spectators.
Berisha accuses the Socialists of fomenting the violence which engulfed the country of 3.4 million in March and portrays himself and his party as the sole guarantors of stability.

Many Albanians and Western observers say last June's election that gave his Democrats all but a handful of seats was unfair. This time, they face a tough race with the Socialists, heirs to the Communists but now firm advocates of the market.

"Like you, we want free enterprise and private property. It is our historic obligation to make Albania part of Europe," Nano told a rally on Saturday in Kruje, a town half way up a mountain 35 km (20 miles) north of Tirana.
Predicting the outcome is virtually impossible in a country with no real opinion polls and big disparities between cities and countryside. But Socialist rallies have had larger crowds.

Berisha was forced to call the early poll at the height of the March rebellion. Rioters looted weapons from depots and for several days, with army and police absent, Albania perched on the brink of anarchy. Some 1,500 people have been killed.

Berisha also had to appoint a multi-party government led by the Socialists. A multi-national peacekeeping force of 7,000 was dispatched to restore a degree of order but gangs still roam many roads and some areas elude control of authorities.
After weeks of doubts about whether conditions were right to stage the vote, all parties have agreed to sign an agreement on Monday in Rome to ensure it proceeds freely and peacefully.
First elected in 1992 by parliament, Berisha won the backing of the United States for his pro-market policies and initially achieved some of Eastern Europe's best results.

But he ignored warnings of impending catastrophe with the rise of pyramid investment schemes. Western support ebbed away as he took authoritarian measures, including his re-election in March a day after the proclamation of a state of emergency.
An overnight curfew remains in place and violence is still commonplace. Several dozen people were killed in the past week.
In the latest incident, a senior Democratic Party official was seized for several hours by armed men in Sarande, one of the focal points of the rebellion near the Greek border.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe, with some 500 observers overseeing the vote, is confident of fairly normal conditions, but questions remain on procedures.
